title: Attachment Styles in Relationships: The 4 Types Explained — cv.cm
description: The four attachment styles in adult relationships: secure, anxious, avoidant, fearful-avoidant. How each acts in dating and conflict, and how styles change.
h1: What are the four attachment styles in relationships?
answer: Attachment styles describe how people handle closeness and the fear of losing it. The four usual types are secure (comfortable with closeness), anxious (worried about being left), avoidant (uncomfortable depending on others) and fearful-avoidant (wanting closeness but afraid of it). Researchers now see them as two scales, anxiety and avoidance, rather than fixed boxes, and they can change over time.

body: No style makes you a good or bad person. Each one is a way of staying safe that made sense at some point in your life.

Psychiatrist John Bowlby developed attachment theory to explain the strong bond between infants and the people who care for them. Psychologist Mary Ainsworth later expanded it and observed that infants show different patterns, such as secure or anxious, depending on how reliably caregivers respond to them.

In 1987, Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver proposed that adult romantic love works partly through the same attachment system. Adults, like children, feel safer when a partner is close and responsive and feel distress when the partner seems unavailable. Later work by Brennan, Clark and Shaver found two main dimensions behind the styles: attachment anxiety (worry about whether a partner will be there) and attachment avoidance (discomfort with depending on others or opening up). Secure people are low on both.
This matters for how you use the idea. You are not one fixed type. You have a position on two scales, and that position can shift with different partners and over the years.

body: These are tendencies, not rules. Stress, culture and the specific partner all change how someone acts. In cultures where people show feelings less openly, calm or reserved behavior is not automatically avoidance.

A common painful pattern happens when one partner leans anxious and the other leans avoidant. The anxious partner feels distance and reaches out more: more messages, more questions, more need to talk. The avoidant partner feels pressure and pulls back: shorter replies, more time alone. That distance makes the anxious partner more worried, and the cycle tightens.

ol: Trigger: a slow reply, a cancelled plan, a cold tone.
The anxious partner pursues: "Why are you being distant? Are we okay?"
The avoidant partner withdraws: "I'm fine. I just need some space."
The anxious partner feels rejected and pushes harder.
The avoidant partner feels trapped and pulls further away.

body: Neither person is the villain. Each is trying to feel safe in their own way. The way out is for both to see the cycle as the problem, not each other. The anxious partner learns to calm down before reaching out. The avoidant partner learns to give a short, warm signal before taking space, such as "I need an hour to myself. I'm not upset with you. I'll call you at 9."
This pattern can look like mixed signals or the silent treatment. Those articles on this shelf cover what to say in more detail.

Yes, to a degree. Bowlby himself thought a person's pattern could change when new relationship experiences did not match old expectations. Research finds only moderate stability over time, and the link between childhood attachment and adult romantic attachment is real but modest. Psychologists still do not fully understand exactly what makes a style change.

Clinicians use the term earned security for adults who had difficult early relationships but became secure later, often through a stable partner, close friendships, therapy or making sense of their own story. Change usually comes from repeated new experiences, not from reading about styles once.
cv.cm's attachment style test can help you see your own pattern as a starting point. Treat the result as a mirror, not a label.

ol: Notice the alarm. When a reply is slow, name it to yourself: "My attachment alarm is going off. It does not mean I'm being left."
Wait before you send a second message. Do something calming for twenty or thirty minutes first.
Ask for what you need directly instead of testing: "It helps me when you say good night if you're going to be offline."
Choose partners whose actions are consistent. Steady people can feel less exciting at first; that calm is not boredom.
Build a life with many supports: friends, family, hobbies, sleep. Your partner does not have to be your only source of safety.
Notice the urge to escape when things get close, and name it instead of acting on it right away.
Take space with words: say how long you need and when you will come back.
Share one small feeling a day, even something simple like "I missed you today."
Look for the real reason behind the urge to leave. Is the partner doing something wrong, or is closeness itself uncomfortable?
Remember that depending on someone a little is not weakness. Secure people rely on each other and still keep their independence.

sections.h: How to talk about needs with a partner
body: Talking about attachment works best in a calm moment and focuses on what helps, not on diagnosing each other.

ul: "When I don't hear from you for a whole day, I start to worry. A short message helps me a lot."
"When we argue, I need a short break before I can think clearly. If I say I'll come back in thirty minutes, I will."
"What helps you feel close to me? What makes you feel crowded?"
"Can we agree on a signal for when one of us needs a pause?"

body.note: Avoid using styles as insults, such as "You're just avoidant". Labels end conversations. Specific needs start them.

body: If insecurity comes with fear, control or abuse, attachment is not the main issue. See the red flags article, and contact a local support service if you feel unsafe.

faq.q: What is the rarest attachment style?
faq.a: Fearful-avoidant is usually described as the least common in community samples, and secure as the most common. Exact percentages vary between studies and countries, so treat any single number with caution.

faq.q: Can two avoidant people have a good relationship?
faq.a: They can, especially if both value independence and talk openly about it. The risk is drifting apart, so it helps to plan regular time together and to check in about feelings on purpose.

faq.q: Is attachment style caused by parents?
faq.a: Early care matters, but it is not the only cause. Later relationships, life events, temperament and culture all play a part, and adult experiences can change your style.

faq.q: How do I know my attachment style?
faq.a: Look at how you act when a partner is distant or when you argue, and how comfortable you are depending on others. A questionnaire based on the anxiety and avoidance scales can give you a rough picture.

faq.q: Does an anxious attachment style mean I am needy?
faq.a: No. It means your system is sensitive to signs of distance. Needing reassurance is human. With clear communication and a steady partner, many anxious people feel much calmer.
